Learning Objectives

INTRODUCTORY CHAPTER

By the end of this lecture you should be able to recognise, classify, and initiate management for the common anorectal presentations — and flag the ones that should never be labelled benign on first encounter.

01 AnatomyDescribe the surgical anatomy of the anal canal and pelvic floor relevant to anorectal disease.
02 AssessmentTake a focused history and perform a systematic anorectal examination — including DRE and anoscopy.
03 RecognitionRecognise the presentation and classify common benign anorectal conditions.
04 ManagementOutline the medical and surgical management ladder for each major disorder.
05 Red flagsIdentify red-flag features that mandate urgent referral or biopsy.
06 DifferentialDistinguish anorectal disease from its key differentials — malignancy and IBD.

Introduction

Speaker notes

Good morning, everyone. Welcome back to Surgery 453. Today we're talking about anorectal disorders — a topic that feels awkward to discuss but that you will manage constantly as junior doctors, on call, in clinic, and in the emergency room. Patients are often embarrassed to bring these complaints up, so part of our job is making it easy for them to talk to us.

Six objectives, but really one habit I want you to leave with: never let the word 'haemorrhoids' end your thinking. It's the most over-used label in this whole area of medicine, and it's often wrong. Keep that in the back of your mind through everything we cover today.

I

Anatomy & Clinical Assessment

The foundation every anorectal diagnosis rests on: anatomy first, then a careful history, then a structured examination.

2 · Pelvic floor & spaces

Anatomy & Clinical Assessment

Speaker notes

Let's start where every good clinician starts — with the anatomy. I know some of you find this the dry part, but stay with me: almost every question you'll ever get asked about this region comes back to one line, the dentate line. Get comfortable with it now and the rest of the lecture will feel like common sense.

SECTION I · ANATOMY

Surgical Anatomy of the Anal Canal

Five landmarks every exam answer starts from. Memorise these and the rest of the lecture is pattern recognition.

1 · Anal canal3–4 cm long, extends from the anorectal ring to the anal verge.
2 · Dentate lineDivides embryological hindgut (columnar, insensate) from proctoderm (squamous, somatically innervated) — the deciding landmark for pain, staging, and lymphatic drainage.
3 · Internal sphincterInvoluntary smooth muscle, continuation of the rectal circular muscle; maintains resting tone (~70–85% of resting pressure).
4 · External sphincterVoluntary striated muscle, deep/superficial/subcutaneous parts, continuous with puborectalis; generates squeeze pressure.
5 · Anorectal ringPalpable muscular ring (puborectalis + upper sphincters) at the apex of the canal — division causes incontinence.

Perianal & Perirectal Spaces

Ischiorectal, intersphincteric, and supralevator spaces — where cryptoglandular sepsis spreads.

Pelvic Floor (view from below)

Puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, and coccygeus forming the pelvic diaphragm.

Puborectalis maintains the anorectal angle at rest; the ischiorectal and intersphincteric spaces are continuous with the perianal space — the routes an abscess follows.

Anal canal in cross-section: sphincter complex, anal glands, and dentate line landmarks.

Speaker notes

Picture this cross-section every time a patient describes a symptom to you — it becomes your mental map. Notice the anal glands sitting right at the dentate line; hold onto that image, because that's exactly where abscesses and fistulas begin. We'll come back to it later in the lecture.

Notes

Anal Canal Anatomy

The anal canal is the terminal part of the GI tract, extending from the anal verge (the external opening) to the anorectal junction. Almost every symptom, sign and complication in this lecture is explained by two anatomical facts: the position of the dentate line, and the arrangement of the sphincter complex.

~4 cm Anal canal length (male)·−1 cm Shorter in females·~2 cm Maximal anal dilatation·~500 mL Normal rectal capacity
Notes

Structural Landmarks

Anorectal ring — the tight ring felt on DRE, formed by puborectalis +

internal anal sphincter + external anal sphincter.

Anal columns — longitudinal folds created by the transition from the

wide rectum to the narrow canal.

Rectal wall layers — mucosa → submucosa → muscular layer →

adventitia/serosa.

Dentate line — divides the canal into upper and lower parts and

explains the differences in sensation and symptoms.

Anal glands — open at the lower ends of the columns, around the

dentate line; secrete mucus to ease stool passage.

Resting shape — the rectum is capacious; the anal canal is normally slit-

like at rest.

Notes

The Perianal Spaces

SpaceBoundaries / Significance
IntersphinctericLies between the internal and external sphincters. Tight and narrow — abscess here is disproportionately painful; it is also the plane of the commonest fistula type.
Ischioanal (ischiorectal)Outside the sphincter complex, between the anal canal and the surrounding pelvic bone and soft tissue. Large space — pathology here may be completely invisible on inspection.
SupralevatorDeep, above the levator plate. Abscess here presents with constitutional symptoms rather than obvious local findings.
WHY FEMALE ANATOMY MATTERS
The anterior anal canal / sphincter segment is shorter in women, so there is a greater risk of faecal incontinence after any anorectal surgery. Weigh this carefully before sphincterotomy or haemorrhoidectomy in a female patient.
THE PALPATION RULE
Always palpate, even when inspection is normal. The ischioanal space is large enough to hide an abscess or mass with no external abnormality at all.
Notes

The Dentate Line — The Single Most Useful Landmark

FeatureAbove the Dentate LineBelow the Dentate Line
SensationVisceral — relatively insensateSomatic — highly sensitive
Pain from lesionsDull or absentSharp, severe, well localised
HaemorrhoidsInternal — graded I–IV by prolapseExternal — no grading system
FissureNot the site of a typical fissureSite of all anal fissures
Fistula terminologyDescribed as a high fistulaDescribed as a low fistula
SphincterotomyDivision must not extend to hereDivision stops below the dentate line
RULE OF THUMB
If the presentation is painful, the lesion is almost always below the dentate line (fissure, external/thrombosed haemorrhoid, abscess). If it is painless bleeding, think above the dentate line (internal haemorrhoid) — but only after excluding malignancy.
Painless bleeding → think above the line. Painful bleeding → think below the line.
Notes

Continence

The main function of the anorectal complex is controlled defecation at an appropriate time and place. Continence is not a single muscle — it is the sum of four contributions.

DETERMINANTS OF CONTINENCE
Internal anal sphincter Smooth, involuntary Continuous resting closure 70–80% of resting tone·External anal sphincter Skeletal, voluntary Fatigable Pudendal nerve·Puborectalis / levator ani Maintains the anorectal angle Part of the anorectal ring·Rectal reservoir Capacity ~500 mL Compliance matters as much as muscle
REDUCED CAPACITY = URGENCY
Colitis, proctitis and radiation injury reduce rectal capacity and compliance. The sphincters may be perfectly intact, yet the patient still cannot hold stool. Urgency with normal sphincter tone points at the reservoir, not the muscle.

Blood Supply, Lymphatics & Innervation

The dentate line is the watershed for arterial supply, venous drainage, lymphatics, and sensation — and for how disease on each side behaves.

FeaturesAbove the dentate lineBelow the dentate line
EpitheliumColumnarSquamous
Arterial supplySuperior rectal artery (IMA)Inferior rectal artery (internal pudendal)
Venous drainageSuperior rectal vein → portal systemInferior rectal vein → systemic (caval) system
LymphaticsInferior mesenteric / internal iliac nodesSuperficial inguinal nodes
SensationVisceral (stretch only) — autonomicSomatic — richly pain-sensitive
Clinical pointInternal haemorrhoids here are painlessFissures and thrombosed external piles here are painful

Clinical rule: painless bleeding → think above the line Painful bleeding → think below the line.

Dentate line

Speaker notes

If you remember nothing else from this table, remember this one sentence: does it hurt or not? A patient who says the bleeding is completely painless is telling you, without realising it, that the problem is above the dentate line. A patient wincing every time they sit down is telling you it's below. That single question will get you most of the way to a diagnosis before you've even examined them.

SECTION I · ASSESSMENT

History Taking & Red Flags

Characterise the symptom, then screen for features that change the differential.

Characterise the Symptom

  • Bleeding
  • Colour, timing (on paper / dripping / mixed in stool), relation to defecation.
  • Pain
  • Constant vs defecation-related, sitting tolerance; nocturnal pain suggests sepsis.
  • , Discharge, Itching, Soiling
  • Onset, reducibility, hygiene impact, continence.

Red Flags

Bowel Habit Change & Constitutional Symptoms

Bowel habit change, weight loss, tenesmus, family history…………….. Warrant colonoscopy.

Age > 50, Anaemia, Palpable Mass

Always exclude cancer before labeling as “hemorrhoids.”

If in Doubt

Anaemia + age > 45 + bleeding of any kind → colonoscopy.

Speaker notes

Try running through this in your head the next time a patient tells you they've 'just got piles.' Ask them to describe the blood — on the tissue, dripping into the bowl, or mixed through the stool — because each of those tells a slightly different story. And if a middle-aged patient walks in with new bleeding, get in the habit of asking yourself out loud, 'what am I missing if this isn't haemorrhoids?' That question has saved careers.

Red flags: bowel-habit change, weight loss, tenesmus, family history → colonoscopy. Age > 50, anaemia, palpable mass → always exclude cancer before labelling "haemorrhoids". Anaemia + age > 45 + bleeding of any kind → colonoscopy.
  • 20-year-old with 3rd-degree haemorrhoids, family history of colon cancer and iron-deficiency anaemia → colonoscopy. 439 ×12

Key Diagnostic Symptoms

SECTION I · ASSESSMENT

Three core symptoms. The dominant one usually steers your first move, and tells you where to look.

  • 1 · Bright-red blood on toilet paper or dripping into the bowl usually points to:

1. A low anorectal source

Rectal Bleeding2. Haemorrhoids

3. Fissure

  • Dark or maroon blood needs evaluation for proximal GI bleeding.

Bedside rule: bright red on wiping means a distal source. Dark or mixed-in blood means colonoscopy to exclude a proximal lesion.

Notes

Assessment of Anorectal Symptoms

Rectal Bleeding — Ask About Colour, Timing and Mixing

Character of BleedingLikely LevelThink Of
Bright red, at the end of defecation or on the toilet paperDistal anorectalHaemorrhoid, anal fissure
Dark maroon or clottedAbove the anal canalMore proximal colonic source

2 of 3

Three core symptoms. The dominant one usually steers your first move, and tells you where to look.

2 · Anorectal Pain

  • Sharp, tearing pain with defecation indicates a fissure.
  • Constant, severe, throbbing pain suggests:
    • 1. Thrombosed haemorrhoid
    • 2. Anorectal abscess
  • Examine before you reassure.

Bedside rule: pain only with defecation means a fissure. Constant throbbing pain means an abscess. Examine before you reassure.

Notes

Pain — The Character Localises the Lesion

Sharp / tearing pain with defecation → anal fissure. This is the classic descriptor.
Constant, severe, throbbing pain → perianal or anorectal abscess, thrombosed or complicated haemorrhoid, or an inflammatory / malignant lesion.
Any pain at all implies a lesion below the dentate line, where the mucosa is somatically innervated.

SECTION I · ASSESSMENT

Three core symptoms. The dominant one usually steers your first move, and tells you where to look.

  • 3 · Distinguish reducible tissue from circumferential full-thickness tissue:

1. Reducible: prolapsing internal haemorrhoids

Mass / Prolapse2. Circumferential, full-thickness: rectal prolapse
  • A painful fixed mass:

1. Think abscess first

2. Neoplasm second

Bedside rule: a reducible mass is usually haemorrhoidal, a circumferential rosette is rectal prolapse, a painful fixed mass is an abscess until proven otherwise.

Notes

Lump, Discharge, Itching and Soiling

FindingInterpretation
Reducible lumpHaemorrhoid is likely — ask whether it reduces spontaneously or needs to be pushed back
Full-thickness prolapsing massConsider rectal prolapse
Fixed, full, irreducible massConsider abscess or malignancy
DischargeConsider fistula or abscess
Itching / soilingLeakage or discharge; also seen with prolapsing haemorrhoids
RED FLAGS — DO NOT DIAGNOSE HAEMORRHOIDS OR FISSURE WITHOUT EXAMINING
Change in bowel habit plus constitutional symptoms: lethargy, weight loss, anorexia.
New anorectal symptoms or pain in an older patient.
Anaemia.
Palpable mass on DRE.
THE PROFESSOR'S AGE THRESHOLDS — HIGH YIELD
>50 years with new pain or symptoms — investigate endoscopically even if a fissure is visible.
>45 years + anaemia → colonoscopy.
>45 years + rectal bleeding or constitutional symptoms → evaluate the rectum and colon, because of possible malignancy.
SECTION I · ASSESSMENT

Examination, DRE & Investigations

Document every finding by clock position with the patient in lithotomy.

1 · Positioning & inspectionLeft lateral (Sims) or lithotomy, good lighting, chaperone present. Inspect perianal skin, fissures, fistula openings, skin tags, prolapse — ask the patient to strain.
2 · Digital rectal exam (DRE)Sphincter tone, masses, tenderness, prostate; document findings by clock position.
3 · Anoscopy / proctoscopyVisualises haemorrhoidal cushions and the dentate line — DRE alone misses most internal haemorrhoids.
4 · Sigmoidoscopy / colonoscopyRigid or flexible; indicated for bleeding with red-flag features or age > 45–50.

Anoscopy / proctoscopy set-up for direct visualisation of the anal canal.

Speaker notes

A quick word on bedside manner here, because this exam makes people understandably anxious. Explain each step before you do it, always have a chaperone, and keep your patient talking — it relaxes the sphincter and makes your exam more accurate, not just kinder. And remember: a normal DRE does not rule out internal haemorrhoids. You need the anoscope to actually see them.

  • Left lateral fissure with skin tags and a relaxed sphincter → biopsy under anaesthesia (atypical fissure). 438 ×3
Notes

Anorectal Examination

THE FOUR-STEP EXAMINATION
1 · Prepare Good light source Gloves, lubricant Local anaesthetic if painful Swab for C&S if pus Anoscope / proctoscope·2 · Position Usually left lateral Other positions if simultaneous vaginal exam is needed·3 · Inspect Skin / colour change Erythema External lump Fissure Discharge / opening·4 · Palpate & scope DRE always Anoscopy for the canal Rectosigmoidoscopy if indicated
Notes

Inspection — Know the Normal First

Perianal skin is normally darker, relatively glistening, and less hairy than the surrounding skin. The anal margin is the perianal area extending from that change in skin character toward the anal opening; the anal verge is the opening itself — the start of the anal canal.

Notes

Digital Rectal Examination — What Must Be Assessed

▪Anal opening: normal slit-like vs patulous▪Resting sphincter tone (internal sphincter)
▪Squeeze tone (external sphincter)▪Continuity of the sphincter muscle — prior surgery may have interrupted it
▪Anal canal or rectal mass▪In males, the prostate
TWO PRACTICAL RULES
Do not stop at DRE when symptoms remain unexplained — complete the assessment with endoscopy.
If severe pain prevents an adequate examination, give analgesia / local treatment and re-examine later. Never force the examination.
Notes

Endoscopic Assessment

ModalityReachRole
Anoscopy / proctoscopyAnal canalEvaluates internal canal mucosa and internal haemorrhoids not visible externally — essential for grades I and II
Rectosigmoidoscopy~15–20 cm from the anal vergeAssesses rectum and rectosigmoid junction; particularly important with age >45 + rectal bleeding ± constitutional symptoms

II · Benign Anorectal Disorders

  • Haemorrhoids
  • Anal fissure
  • Anorectal sepsis & fistula
  • Pilonidal disease
  • Anal warts

Haemorrhoids, fissure, sepsis, pilonidal disease and warts — the everyday presentations you will meet on call.

Rt. Anterior · Lt. lateral · Rt. Posterior

Speaker notes

This is the heart of the lecture, and honestly, the heart of your surgical on-call life. These five conditions will make up a huge share of the referrals you get paged about at 2am. Learn this section well and you'll walk into those calls with confidence instead of dread.

SECTION II · HAEMORRHOIDS

Haemorrhoids: Definition & Risk Factors

Downward displacement and engorgement of the normal anal vascular cushions — areas of arteriovenous anastomosis that normally contribute ~15–20% of resting anal pressure and help sense gas, liquid, and solid.

Classic Cushion Positions

Rt. Anterior

Lt. lateral

Rt. Posterior

Risk Factors

  • Habitual

Straining, constipation, low-fibre diet, prolonged sitting, pregnancy, obesity, ageing, family tendency.

  • Pathological

Chronic diarrhoea (IBD), colon malignancy, portal hypertension, spinal injury, rectal surgery, anal intercourse.

Primary cushions cluster at 3, 7, and 11 o'clock in the lithotomy view.

Speaker notes

Here's something that surprises most students: everybody has haemorrhoidal cushions. They're normal anatomy, doing a real job in continence. Disease is simply what happens when those cushions get pushed too far, too often. So when a patient asks you 'why me,' you can honestly tell them it's usually just years of straining and pressure catching up with completely normal tissue.

Notes

Haemorrhoids

Haemorrhoids are the downward displacement and enlargement of the normal anal vascular cushions. The cushions are composed of a mixed arteriovenous plexus and are normally held in place by suspensory tissue and ligaments; repeated straining stretches that support, allowing the cushions to descend and prolapse. The blood supply comes from the superior, middle and inferior haemorrhoidal arteries.

Notes

Risk Factors

Constipation and straining — the central mechanism
Low fluid intake
Prolonged sitting
Obesity
Chronic disease
Portal hypertension

Pregnancy

ON "FAMILY HISTORY"
A family tendency usually reflects shared family habits and lifestyle — diet, fluid intake, activity — rather than genuine genetic inheritance.

Haemorrhoids: Pathogenesis

Three structural changes, driven by three physiological mechanisms.

Structural ChangesInternal vs External
  • Dilated cushions of the arteriovenous plexus
  • Stretched suspensory fibromuscular stroma
  • Prolapsed rectal mucosa

Internal cushions above, external cushions below the dentate line.

Speaker notes

Don't try to memorise this as three unrelated facts — it's really one story told three times. Pressure goes up, the tissue holding the cushions in place stretches out, and eventually the mucosa itself starts to prolapse. Once you see it as a single sequence rather than a list, it's much easier to recall under exam pressure.

Clinical Features & Differentials

Internal cushions arise above the dentate line and bleed painlessly; external cushions arise below it and can be acutely painful.

Clinical FeaturesDifferentials to Exclude
Painless bright-red bleedingCommonly associated with defecation.Anal fissure pain-predominant, posterior tear
Prolapse with increase in sizeMay protrude down with straining.Rectal prolapse circumferential, concentric rings
Mucoid discharge & pruritus aniMucus release causes local irritation.Perianal / anorectal abscess painful fixed mass
Pain if complications superveneStrangulation, thrombosis, or abscess.Colorectal malignancy always exclude if age > 45–50 or red flags
Speaker notes

This right-hand list is the one I actually want you to remember from this slide, more than the features on the left. Anyone can spot a haemorrhoid. What separates a good clinician from a dangerous one is pausing, every single time, to ask what else this could be before you write 'haemorrhoids' in the notes.

Notes

Clinical Features

The classic presentation is painless bright-red bleeding. As prolapse increases, the patient develops a lump, discharge or soiling, and pruritus.

BLEEDING PLUS SIGNIFICANT PAIN IS NOT A SIMPLE HAEMORRHOID
Reconsider the diagnosis and think of: anal fissure · thrombosed haemorrhoid · infected, incarcerated or strangulated haemorrhoid · inflammatory bowel disease · malignancy.
FOUR QUESTIONS TO ASK ABOUT THE LUMP
1. Is there a lump at all?
2. What is its relation to the bowel movement?
3. Does it disappear or reduce spontaneously?
4. Is there pain?
The answers alone will usually give you the grade. Differential diagnosis: anal fissure, rectal prolapse, perianal abscess, malignancy — and in patients >45 years, malignancy must stay on the list.

Speaker notes

This grading table is genuinely one of the highest-yield things in the whole lecture — it comes up in exams constantly, and more importantly, it's exactly how you'll actually decide treatment on the wards. Here's a trick that helps students remember it: ask 'does it come back on its own, does the patient have to push it back, or does it never go back at all?' Walk through that question and the grade almost answers itself.

  • Haemorrhoids that can be manually reduced → grade 3. 438
Notes

Classification

Type / GradeDefinitionHow It Is FoundTypical Management
ExternalBelow the dentate lineVisible on inspectionNo grading system exists
Grade IBleeding without prolapseUsually not seen externally — diagnosed by anoscopyConservative ± laser for persistent bleeding
Grade IIProlapses with straining, then reduces spontaneouslyOften requires anoscopyConservative, band ligation, laser

STEP 1 · CONSERVATIVE — FIRST-LINE FOR ALL HAEMORRHOIDS
Lifestyle modification: sedentary → more active
High-fibre diet and increased water intake
Stool softener
Topical agents
Venoactive treatment for bleeding, e.g. Daflon
STEP 2 · OFFICE PROCEDURES
Rubber-band ligation — the workhorse office procedure.
Sclerotherapy — used infrequently, particularly when the patient is unfit for or has a contraindication to surgery.
Infrared coagulation — rarely used in the professor's practice; can cause postoperative pain and smelly discharge.
STEP 3 · OPERATIVE
Grade III–IV → haemorrhoidectomy, open or closed excision as appropriate.
Laser therapy — suitable for persistent bleeding in grades I–II, and small grade III after failed conservative therapy. Not for grade IV or large grade III.
HAEMORRHOIDECTOMY — TWO TECHNICAL POINTS THAT PREVENT TWO DISASTERS
Leave bridges of normal mucosa and skin between the excised haemorrhoids → prevents anal stenosis.
Excise the haemorrhoid without injuring the sphincter muscle → prevents faecal incontinence.
COMPLICATED AND ATYPICAL LESIONS
Infected, incarcerated or strangulated haemorrhoidal disease may require operative management, and an associated abscess needs antibiotics when indicated plus incision and drainage. Ulceration or atypical bleeding should prompt a search for underlying disease rather than an assumption of simple haemorrhoids — Crohn disease, syphilis, TB, HIV/AIDS and other infectious or malignant pathology.
Notes

Parks Classification

#TypeCourse of the Tract
1Intersphincteric — most commonEnters the internal sphincter, then travels in the intersphincteric plane between internal and external sphincters
2TranssphinctericPasses through both sphincters

EXTRASPHINCTERIC FISTULA = LOOK FOR A CAUSE
It does not arise from the normal cryptoglandular route, so consider Crohn disease, malignancy, or previous instrumentation / trauma.

Haemorrhoids: Complications

Complications are what turn a painless nuisance into a surgical emergency.

1 · ThrombosisSudden, severe pain from a clotted external pile — excise within 48–72 hours of onset if the patient presents early.
2 · StrangulationGrade IV prolapse with compromised blood supply — irreducible, edematous, at risk of gangrene.
3 · Ulceration & bleedingChronic prolapse can ulcerate; recurrent bleeding may cause iron-deficiency anemia.
4 · Infection / abscessRare, but consider in a hemorrhoid that fails to settle with worsening pain and fever.

Excision of a thrombosed external haemorrhoid under local anaesthetic.

Excision of Thrombosed External Hemorrhoid

  • Anesthetize
  • Make an elliptical incision of skin overlying clot
  • Remove clot
Speaker notes

This is the slide that changes how you triage the on-call patient in genuine agony. Remember that 48-to-72-hour window for a thrombosed pile — miss it, and you're stuck offering sitz baths and analgesia instead of a quick, satisfying excision that will make the patient enormously grateful to you.

Haemorrhoid Management Ladder

1 · Conservative2 · Office procedures3 · Operative4 · Emergency care
High-fibre diet, fluids, stool softeners, topical agents. The basis for every grade.Rubber band ligation (grade I–III), sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation.Excisional haemorrhoidectomy or stapled haemorrhoidopexy for grade III–IV.Thrombosed external pile — excise within 72 h; otherwise analgesia and sitz baths.

Topical nitrates / CCBs are reserved for fissure management — haemorrhoids step up the ladder above.

Speaker notes

Think of this as a ladder you climb one rung at a time, not a menu you pick from. Almost every patient starts at the bottom with fibre and fluids — you'd be amazed how many cases resolve there and never need to see a surgeon at all. Save your operative options for the patients who genuinely need them.

  • Painless bright red bleeding with prolapse that reduces spontaneously (grade II), no red flags → keyed fibre, stool softeners and topical analgesia (conservative is first-line for every grade; banding next). 442

Surgical & Procedural Techniques

Match technique to grade, band ligation for II to III, excisional haemorrhoidectomy for III to IV or mixed disease, stapling where prolapse dominates, laser for select outpatient cases.

1 · Band ligationOutpatient, targets grade II to III; avoid in patients on anticoagulants.
2 · Open haemorrhoidectomyExcises redundant tissue, wound left open; most effective for grade III to IV.
3 · Stapled haemorrhoidopexyRepositions prolapsing tissue with a circular stapler; less pain, but higher long-term recurrence.
4 · Thrombosed external pileExcise under local anaesthetic if the patient presents within 48 to 72 hours of onset.
5 · Laser haemorrhoidoplastyDiode laser shrinks the vascular cushions with minimal excision; quicker recovery, but higher cost and less long-term data.
6 · Operative principlePreserve anoderm bridges between excision sites to reduce the risk of anal stenosis.

Pictures: Band ligation · Open haemorrhoidectomy (Ferguson) · Stapled haemorrhoidopexy · Thrombosed external pile, excision

Haemorrhoidectomy: preserve anoderm/skin bridges between excisions → prevents anal stenosis; spare the sphincter → prevents incontinence.
SECTION II · ANAL FISSURE

Anal Fissure: Definition & Risk Profile

A linear ulcer of the lower anal canal, classically in the posterior midline.

1 · DefinitionA linear ulcer involving the lower half of the anal canal.
2 · LocationUsually the posterior commissure, in the midline.
3 · Typical patientMore common in men than women, and in younger than older patients.

Skews male and skews young, though fissures occur at any age.

Anatomy: internal/external anal sphincter and fissure site. · Clinical photo: fissure at the posterior midline.

The slide says fissures are more common in men and in the young; the doctor's spoken notes say more common in women (and in the young — stronger sphincter). Both agree it is a disease of younger patients; for "fissure vs fistula" pairs, the notes contrast fissure: female > male with fistula: male > female.
Notes

Anal Fissure

An anal fissure is a linear tear or ulcer of the lower anal canal, below the dentate line. It is more common in women, and more common in younger patients — attributed to a stronger, more active sphincter muscle. Causes include hard stool and constipation, but also diarrhoea, and instrumentation or trauma.

Anal Fissure: Pathophysiology & Presentation

A linear tear in the anoderm distal to the dentate line, most commonly in the posterior midline.

1 · Trigger → spasm → chronicityHard stool trauma tears the anoderm; internal sphincter spasm follows, reducing anodermal blood flow; ischaemia perpetuates the tear and prevents healing.
2 · Classic triadSevere pain on defecation, bright-red bleeding, a visible tear on gentle inspection.
3 · Chronic fissureOedema (sentinel pile), hypertrophied papilla, visible internal sphincter fibres at the base.
4 · Off-midline fissuresAtypical location — think Crohn's, tuberculosis, HIV, or malignancy.

Internal / external sphincter anatomy and the resulting anal fissure.

Speaker notes

Ask any patient with an acute fissure to describe the pain and they'll usually say it feels like passing broken glass. That vivid a description is almost diagnostic on its own, before you've even examined them. And remember the vicious cycle here — pain causes spasm, spasm causes ischaemia, ischaemia prevents healing — which is exactly why so many patients start avoiding the toilet altogether and make things worse.

Notes

Pathophysiology — The Vicious Cycle

TEAR BELOW THE DENTATE LINE → EXPOSED SOMATIC NERVE ENDINGS
1 · Severe pain Sensitive somatic endings are exposed directly to stool and stretch.·2 · Spinal reflex Pain triggers a reflex internal sphincter spasm.·3 · Second pain component The intense sphincter contraction itself hurts — spasm may last ~4 hours after defecation.·4 · Ischaemia Persistent spasm reduces perfusion, oxygen and nutrient delivery → impaired healing.
WHY THIS EXPLAINS THE WHOLE TREATMENT STRATEGY
Pain has two components: exposed sensory nerves, and sphincter spasm. Every treatment that works — topical relaxants, Botox, sphincterotomy — works by breaking the spasm and restoring perfusion so the fissure can heal.
Notes

Core goal: eradicate the tract while preserving continence — the amount of sphincter crossed dictates the approach.

Speaker notes

Every fistula operation is really a negotiation between two competing goals — curing the sepsis and protecting continence — and the amount of muscle the tract crosses is what tips that balance one way or the other. A 28-year-old man who lifts heavy weights presents with bright-red, painless rectal bleeding and a reducible mass at 3 o'clock. Which structure is most likely engorged?

b.Perianal skin tag complex
c.Internal haemorrhoidal cushion
d.Anal transitional zone epithelium

The internal haemorrhoidal cushion sits above the dentate line. Because this region is viscerally innervated, engorgement or pathology here is typically painless. Anorectal Anatomy
1. Overview

The anatomy of the anus and rectum is critical for understanding the evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of anorectal disorders. The key anatomical structures include the external and internal surfaces, sphincter muscles, vascular supply, lymphatic drainage, and innervation.

2. Surface Anatomy
A. External to Internal Structures
1. Gluteal Skin (Perianal Region)
  • Contains hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands.
  • Common disorders:
    • Anal condyloma (HPV infection)
    • Perianal hidradenitis suppurativa (involves apocrine sweat glands; does not occur in the anal canal).

2. Anoderm (Anal Canal)

  • Begins at the anal verge and ends at the dentate line.
  • Devoid of hair and sweat glands.
  • Highly innervated (somatic nerves) → Pain-sensitive.
  • Common conditions:
    • Anal fissures (often accompanied by a sentinel tag and hypertrophied anal papilla).
    • Anal stenosis (post-hemorrhoidectomy or excessive anoderm excision).

3. Anal Transitional Zone

  • Lies between the anoderm and rectal mucosa.
  • Contains squamous, cuboidal, transitional, and columnar epithelium.
  • Columnae of Morgagni: Vertical ridges in the anal canal.
  • Anal Crypts & Glands:
    • Originate here and extend variably into deeper tissues.
    • Common site of infection → Leads to anal abscesses & fistulas.

4. Rectal Mucosa

  • Begins above the dentate line.
  • Contains engorged vessels responsible for internal hemorrhoids.
  • Viscerally innervated (not pain-sensitive).

A. Hemorrhoids
  • Internal hemorrhoids:
  • Above the dentate line (painless).
  • Commonly prolapse & bleed.
  • Can be treated with rubber band ligation.
  • External hemorrhoids:
  • Below the dentate line (painful).
  • Requires anesthesia for surgical excision.
B. Anal Fistulas & Abscesses
  • Originate from blocked anal glands in the crypts.
  • Can lead to perianal, intersphincteric, or ischiorectal abscesses.
C. Rectal Prolapse vs. Hemorrhoidal Prolapse
  • Hemorrhoidal prolapse:
  • Radial folds seen on examination.
  • Rectal prolapse:
  • Circumferential folds.
D. Fecal Incontinence
  • Causes:
  • Childbirth trauma (affects EAS).
  • Neurologic diseases (MS, diabetes, scleroderma).
  • Surgical injury (sphincterotomy, fistulotomy).
  • Evaluation:
  • Endoanal ultrasound to assess sphincter integrity.
  • Surgical Management:
  • Sphincter repair for injuries.
  • Sphincter-sparing techniques for complex fistulas.
E. Pudendal Nerve Injury
  • Results in loss of voluntary anal sphincter control.
  • Occurs with pelvic surgery or prolonged vaginal delivery.

A. Office-Based Procedures
1. Rubber Band Ligation (Preferred)
  • Best for Grades I-III
  • Rubber band placed above dentate line → ischemia → hemorrhoid sloughs in 5-10 days.
  • Complications: Rare sepsis, urinary retention, delayed bleeding.

  • Grades I-II
  • Sclerosing agent (phenol in oil) injected → fibrosis & shrinkage.
  • Complications: Necrosis, perforation.

  • Grades I-II
  • Infrared thermal energy applied to hemorrhoids → shrinkage.
  • Complications: Bleeding, necrosis.
B. Surgical Treatment (For Grades III-IV)
1. Excisional Hemorrhoidectomy (Gold Standard)
  • Complete removal of hemorrhoids.
  • Most effective for large, recurrent, Grade III-IV hemorrhoids.
  • Complications:
    • Pain
    • Urinary retention
    • Bleeding
    • Anal stenosis (if excessive tissue removed).

2. Stapled Hemorrhoidopexy

  • Best for circumferential Grade II-III hemorrhoids.
  • Removes redundant mucosa, lifts hemorrhoids.
  • Less pain, but higher recurrence rate.
  • Unique complications: Rectovaginal fistula, rectal obstruction.

3. Doppler-Guided Hemorrhoidectomy

  • Ligation of hemorrhoidal arteries using Doppler guidance.
  • Preserves mucosa, less pain than excisional surgery.
  • Long-term efficacy still under study.

  • Avoid prolonged sitting/straining
  • Regular exercise
  • Limit time on the toilet
  • Prognosis:
  • Lifestyle modifications reduce recurrence.
  • Office-based procedures (banding, sclerotherapy) effective for Grades I-III.

1. Definition and Pathophysiology
  • Anal fissure: A tear in the anoderm (lining of the anal canal).
  • Typically found in the posterior (90%) or anterior (10%) midline.
  • Caused by trauma (e.g., hard bowel movement) leading to pain, spasm, and impaired healing.
  • Pathogenesis:
  • Trauma → Tear in anoderm → Pain & internal anal sphincter spasm.
  • Increased sphincter pressure → Reduced blood flow → Non-healing ulcer.
  • Forms a vicious cycle of pain, spasm, and ischemia.

Pilonidal Disease
1. Definition and Etiology
  • Pilonidal disease is a chronic infection that occurs in the gluteal cleft (most commonly in the sacrococcygeal region).
  • The term pilonidal means "nest of hair," reflecting its association with hair entrapment.
  • It primarily affects young men (3:1 male-to-female ratio), with a peak incidence between 16-25 years.
  • Risk Factors:
  • Hairy individuals (hair acts as a foreign body).
  • Prolonged sitting (e.g., office workers, drivers).
  • Poor hygiene or excessive sweating.
  • Obesity (increased moisture and friction).
  • Family history (possible genetic predisposition).
2. Pathophysiology
  • The deep gluteal cleft creates a vacuum effect, leading to the suction of loose hairs into the skin pits.
  • The hair and debris in these pits act as foreign bodies, causing chronic inflammation, abscess formation, and sinus tracts.
  • Pilonidal disease can manifest as acute abscesses, chronic draining sinuses, or recurrent non-healing wounds.

1. Anal Cancer
Clinical Findings
  • Rare (~2% of all colorectal malignancies).
  • Histologic subtypes:
  • Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) – most common.
  • Basaloid, mucoepidermoid, epidermoid, and cloacogenic cancers.
  • Risk Factors:
  • HPV infection (HPV-16, HPV-18).
  • HIV, immunosuppression.
  • Anoreceptive intercourse.
  • Tobacco use.
Symptoms
  • Variable presentation (often initially misdiagnosed as benign anorectal disease).
  • Slow-growing tumors.
  • Common symptoms:
  • Pain, bleeding, mass sensation, pruritus, tenesmus, incontinence (advanced cases).
  • Physical Exam:
  • Digital rectal exam (DRE) and anoscopy:
    • Assess tumor size, location, fixation, consistency.
  • Inguinal adenopathy:
    • Palpable nodes should be biopsied (FNA or core biopsy).
  • Imaging & Staging:
  • Endoanal ultrasound & MRI → Primary tumor assessment.
  • CT/PET scan → Distant metastases & nodal involvement.

Treatment Standard Therapy: Chemoradiation (Nigro Protocol)

  • 5-FU + Mitomycin C + Radiation.
  • High response rate (85%-90%).
  • Sphincter preservation.
  • Lower recurrence compared to surgery.
Alternative Approaches
  • Radiation alone (for frail patients).
  • Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) (reduces toxicity).
  • Salvage Surgery (APR - Abdominoperineal Resection)
  • Reserved for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiation.
  • 5-year survival post-APR: 24%-58%.
  • Common complication: Poor wound healing.
Management of Lymph Node Disease
  • Inguinal node involvement:
  • Chemoradiation (90% response rate).
  • Groin dissection NOT routinely recommended unless persistent disease.
Response & Surveillance
  • Response assessed ~8 weeks post-chemoradiation.
  • 85%-90% achieve complete response.
  • Partial response → Close monitoring.
  • Persistent/progressive disease → Biopsy & consider salvage APR.
  • Follow-up:
  • DRE, anoscopy, and inguinal node assessment every 3-6 months (first 2 years), then every 6-12 months (up to 5 years).
  • Routine imaging controversial but commonly done.
Prognosis
  • Complete response rates ~90% for smaller tumors.
  • 5-year survival:
  • Small tumors: 70%-90%.
  • Advanced/recurrent disease: 24%-58% (post-APR).
